# About this document {.unnumbered}

This document is a reference analysis for the author, not a course page. It shows what
students could do with these data with the tools of Chapters 1 to 7 (RTMB, RTMBdist,
DHARMa and TMB), and follows the structure of Case study 2: the data, an exploration, the
model, the choice of curve, distribution and random effect, the candidates for the effect
of the degradation class, the answer, checks of the model and a simulation of the estimator.
Alternatives are in boxes titled "Alternative" and traps in boxes titled "Pitfall";
@sec-summary lists them all. `README.md` in this folder describes the source of the data,
the paper, the dissertation from which the data come (Omuto 2006) and what is still not
known about the data; `data_description.md` describes the study for students.

::: {.callout-note title="Possible research question (for the author to decide)"}
Do the plots of the three degradation classes take up different amounts of water, and does the
way their infiltration rate declines differ? The answer below is the ratio of the typical
depth of water that infiltrates in the first 30 minutes, a quantity within the range of
every run.
:::

The document needs RTMB, RTMBdist, DHARMa, TMB and knitr (HydroMe is not needed: the data
are in the CSV) and takes about a minute to render, most of it in the simulation of
@sec-simulation. The optimisations are deterministic and every simulation has its own
seed. Numbers in the text are calculated inline from the code, except descriptions of
what a figure shows, which were written from the figures of the run of 19 November 2026
(R 4.6.1).

Status: generated draft, not reviewed by the author. Written on 19 November 2026 from the
data and the paper alone; the passages on the study, the measurements and the classes
were updated on 20 November 2026 from the dissertation. The code and the results did not
change.

# The data {#sec-data}

The data come from a survey of physical soil degradation in the Upper Athi River basin
(eastern Kenya) between December 2002 and March 2003 (Omuto 2006, Chapter 3). Infiltration
was measured with a single-ring infiltrometer (inner diameter 30 cm) on a pre-wetted soil
surface by the falling-head method: the fall of the water level in the ring was read at
successive times. The survey measured 180 plots of 30 m × 30 m in 45 randomly placed
blocks of 1 km², four plots per block, at three positions per plot (P1, P2 and P3, at 5,
15 and 25 m along the slope). Before the measurements each plot was assigned by eye to one
of three classes of physical degradation:

- `E0`, non-degraded: no visible sign of degradation;
- `E1`, moderately degraded: signs of degradation of the soil in place (a surface crust or
  seal, compaction);
- `E2`, severely degraded: several signs, including erosion (sheet, rill or gully).

The column that holds these classes is called `Erosion`, but only E2 involves erosion, so
this document speaks of **degradation classes**.

The file contains 1,105 readings of the infiltration rate (`Rate`, cm/min) over successive
time intervals (`Time`, min, the end of the interval) on 30 plots (`PlotNo`) in the three
classes (`Erosion`: E0, E1, E2). `Sample` is the row number and `Cumrate` the running sum
of `Rate` within a plot (@sec-reading shows that it is not a depth).

```{r}
infil = read.csv("infiltration.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
str(infil)
```

`read.csv()` orders the levels of `PlotNo` alphabetically (`10lP3` before `1lP3`). We
order them by plot number instead, which is also the order of the rows in the file
(sorted by plot and time). E0 is the reference level of `Erosion`.

```{r}
infil$PlotNo = factor(infil$PlotNo, levels = unique(infil$PlotNo))
levels(infil$Erosion)

# Colours (Okabe-Ito) and symbols of the three degradation classes.
erosion_colours = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73")
erosion_symbols = c(1, 19, 17)

# Formatting of numbers quoted in the text.
f1 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
```

# Exploratory data analysis {#sec-eda}

## The design {#sec-design}

The degradation class is a property of the plot, so we first make a table with one row per
plot and count the plots in each class.

```{r}
plots = infil[!duplicated(infil$PlotNo), c("PlotNo", "Erosion")]
n_class = table(plots$Erosion)
n_class
```

There are `r n_class[["E0"]]` plots in E0, `r n_class[["E1"]]` in E1 and only
`r n_class[["E2"]]` in E2. The survey as a whole had 26, 107 and 47 plots in the three
classes (14%, 59% and 26%), so E2 is under-represented here (13%). How the 30 plots were
chosen from the 180 is not documented. Every plot name ends in `lP3`, which probably
means position P3 (25 m along the slope): the data would then be one run at the same
position on each plot. This is our reading of the names; no source says so.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the number of plots, not of readings"}
The class is a property of the plot, so the information about the classes comes from 30
plots, not from 1,105 readings. With `r n_class[["E2"]]` plots in E2, any statement about
E2 rests on four runs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: plots of the same block"}
The survey placed four plots in each block of 1 km², and the data do not say which block a
plot belongs to. If some of the 30 plots share a block, they may be more alike than plots
of different blocks (soil, slope, land use), and the model, which treats the plots as
independent, overstates the information about the classes. Without the block, the data
cannot show whether this matters.
:::

Next, the number of readings per plot, the duration of each run (the time of the last
reading, per plot and its range per class) and the time of the first reading of each plot:

```{r}
n_readings = table(infil$PlotNo)
summary(as.vector(n_readings))
duration = tapply(infil$Time, infil$PlotNo, max)
summary(duration)
tapply(duration, plots$Erosion, range)
first_time = tapply(infil$Time, infil$PlotNo, min)
table(first_time)
```

Runs have `r min(n_readings)` to `r max(n_readings)` readings and last from
`r min(duration)` to `r max(duration)` minutes, with similar ranges in the three classes.
`r sum(first_time == 1)` plots were first read after 1 minute, the other three after 2, 3
and 4 minutes. Every run covers the first `r min(duration)` minutes, which is why the
answer uses the depth infiltrated in the first 30 minutes.

## What a reading is {#sec-reading}

Each reading closes an interval that starts at the previous reading of the same plot (or at
time 0 for the first one). `ave()` applies a function within each plot and returns a vector
in the order of the rows, so it gives the start of every interval:

```{r}
infil$Start = ave(infil$Time, infil$PlotNo, FUN = function(t) c(0, head(t, -1)))
infil$Interval = infil$Time - infil$Start
table(infil$Interval)
```

Readings are taken every minute at first (`r sum(infil$Interval == 1)` intervals) and every
two minutes later (`r sum(infil$Interval == 2)`), with a few longer intervals of 3 to 10
minutes and two of half a minute.

The water that entered the soil during an interval is the rate (cm/min) times the length of
the interval (min), or ten times that in millimetres. It is always a whole number of
millimetres:

```{r}
infil$Drop_mm = infil$Rate * infil$Interval * 10
all(abs(infil$Drop_mm - round(infil$Drop_mm)) < 1e-6)
table(round(infil$Drop_mm))
```

So each `Rate` is a water depth read to the nearest millimetre and divided by the length of
the interval: it is the mean rate over the interval, not the rate at its end. This is what
the falling-head method gives: the fall of the water level in the ring between two
readings (here recorded in whole millimetres), divided by the time between them.

The cumulative depth of infiltrated water (cm) is the running sum of rate times interval.
The column `Cumrate` of the file is the running sum of the rates alone, without the
lengths of the intervals. The second line below checks that, and the third shows the
readings of plot 1lP3 around the change from 1-minute to 2-minute intervals:

```{r}
infil$Depth = ave(infil$Rate * infil$Interval, infil$PlotNo, FUN = cumsum)
all(abs(infil$Cumrate - ave(infil$Rate, infil$PlotNo, FUN = cumsum)) < 1e-6)
infil[infil$PlotNo == "1lP3", c("Time", "Interval", "Rate", "Cumrate", "Depth")][18:24, ]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: Cumrate is not the cumulative infiltration"}
`Cumrate` equals `Depth` while the intervals last 1 minute and falls behind as soon as they
last 2 minutes (at 28 min in plot 1lP3: 27.6 against 30.8 cm). A student who fits a
cumulative infiltration equation (Philip's $I(t) = S\sqrt{t} + At$, or the integral of
Horton's equation) to `Cumrate` fits the wrong quantity. Use `Depth`, or fit the rates as
below.
:::

The resolution of a reading is the smallest possible change of the rate, one millimetre
over the interval (0.1 cm divided by the interval, in cm/min). Compared with the rates
themselves:

```{r}
infil$Resolution = 0.1 / infil$Interval
summary(infil$Resolution / infil$Rate)
prop_coarse = mean(infil$Resolution / infil$Rate >= 0.25)
prop_coarse
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: coarse readings"}
For `r round(100 * prop_coarse)`% of the readings, one millimetre more or less changes the
rate by a quarter or more. Low rates can only take a few values (0.05, 0.1, 0.15 cm/min
over 2 minutes), which shows as horizontal bands in the figures below and in the residuals.
A continuous distribution treats them as exact; with a coefficient of variation around 0.3
(@sec-spread) this is a rough but usable approximation.
:::

## Infiltration curves of the plots {#sec-curves}

@fig-curves shows the readings of each plot as a line, one panel per degradation class, on the
original scale (top) and the log scale (bottom).

```{r}
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "Infiltration rate against time, one line per plot, on the original (top)
#|   and log (bottom) scale."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (log_axis in c("", "y")) {
  for (e in seq_along(levels(infil$Erosion))) {
    infil_class = infil[infil$Erosion == levels(infil$Erosion)[e], ]
    plot(Rate ~ Time, data = infil_class, type = "n", log = log_axis,
         ylim = range(infil$Rate), main = levels(infil$Erosion)[e],
         xlab = "Time (min)", ylab = "Infiltration rate (cm/min)")
    for (p in unique(as.character(infil_class$PlotNo))) {
      lines(Rate ~ Time, data = infil_class[infil_class$PlotNo == p, ],
            col = erosion_colours[e])
    }
  }
}
par(old_par)
```

In every class the rate falls quickly during the first 10 to 20 minutes and then levels
off, with a lot of noise from reading to reading. The plots differ by more than a factor of
ten in their late rates (0.04 to 0.9 cm/min; @sec-plot-summaries), and on the log scale the
curves of different plots look roughly parallel: a plot that infiltrates fast does so at
every time. This suggests a random effect that multiplies the whole curve of a plot
(@sec-model). Two E0 plots (4lP3, 13lP3) start higher than all but one of the other plots.

@fig-depth shows the cumulative depth against time, all classes in one panel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-depth
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative depth of infiltrated water against time, one line per plot."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
plot(Depth ~ Time, data = infil, type = "n", xlab = "Time (min)",
     ylab = "Cumulative infiltration (cm)")
for (p in levels(infil$PlotNo)) {
  infil_plot = infil[infil$PlotNo == p, ]
  lines(Depth ~ Time, data = infil_plot,
        col = erosion_colours[infil_plot$Erosion[1]])
}
legend("topleft", legend = levels(infil$Erosion), col = erosion_colours, lty = 1,
       bty = "n")
```

The cumulative depths are smooth (the noise of single readings averages out) and become
nearly straight lines after about 20 minutes, with a slope equal to the late rate. The
classes overlap completely.

## Rates that rise at the start {#sec-rises}

The two curves of the paper can only fall. We count the plots whose highest rate is not
their first reading, and print the time of the highest rate in those plots:

```{r}
time_of_max = tapply(seq_len(nrow(infil)), infil$PlotNo,
                     function(rows) infil$Time[rows][which.max(infil$Rate[rows])])
rises = time_of_max > first_time
sum(rises)
time_of_max[rises]
```

In `r sum(rises)` plots the rate rises before it falls, mostly between the first reading
and 2 to 6 minutes (in 5lP3, 6lP3 and 30lP3 the highest reading comes later, at 41, 21 and
13 minutes, a single high reading in a noisy run). Neither curve can rise. The cause is not
known. The surface was wetted before the run, so a dry surface that repels water at first
is an unlikely cause; the settling of the water level after the ring was filled, or air
trapped in the soil, are possible explanations.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Drop the first reading of each plot (@sec-no-first).
:::

## The shape of the decline {#sec-shape}

The paper (Table 1) gives two equations for the rate:

$$
\text{Horton: } f(t) = f_c + (f_0 - f_c)\,e^{-kt},
\qquad
\text{Philip: } f(t) = f_c + \frac{S}{2\sqrt{t}},
$$

where $f_c$ is the steady rate (cm/min), $f_0$ the initial rate (cm/min), $k$ the decay rate
(1/min) and $S$ the sorptivity (cm/min^0.5^). Horton's curve starts at $f_0$ and levels off
at $f_c$. Philip's curve is infinite at $t = 0$ and approaches $f_c$ slowly; it is a straight
line against $1/\sqrt{t}$, with intercept $f_c$ and slope $S/2$. The bottom row of
@fig-curves shows the Horton shape (a fall that flattens on the log scale); @fig-philip
shows the Philip shape.

```{r}
#| label: fig-philip
#| fig-cap: "Infiltration rate against the inverse square root of time, one line per
#|   plot. Philip's equation is a straight line in this figure."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.9
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (e in seq_along(levels(infil$Erosion))) {
  infil_class = infil[infil$Erosion == levels(infil$Erosion)[e], ]
  plot(Rate ~ I(1 / sqrt(Time)), data = infil_class, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 1),
       ylim = range(infil$Rate), main = levels(infil$Erosion)[e],
       xlab = "1 / sqrt(time) (1/min^0.5)", ylab = "Infiltration rate (cm/min)")
  for (p in unique(as.character(infil_class$PlotNo))) {
    lines(Rate ~ I(1 / sqrt(Time)), data = infil_class[infil_class$PlotNo == p, ],
          col = erosion_colours[e])
  }
}
par(old_par)
```

Against $1/\sqrt{t}$ the rates rise from the late readings (left) to the early ones
(right), roughly along straight lines but with much noise, and the first readings
(right-hand end) bend down in the plots with an early rise. Both shapes are plausible from
the figures; the likelihood compares them in @sec-choices. A practical point for students:
Philip's equation is infinite at $t = 0$, so the readings at $t = 1$ min carry a lot of
weight in deciding between the curves.

## One summary per plot {#sec-plot-summaries}

For each plot we calculate the mean rate in the first 5 minutes (early), the mean of the
last five readings (late), their ratio, and the depth infiltrated in the first 30 minutes,
interpolated linearly between readings (every run lasted at least 33 minutes):

```{r}
by_plot = split(infil, infil$PlotNo)
plot_summary = data.frame(
  erosion = sapply(by_plot, function(p) as.character(p$Erosion[1])),
  n = sapply(by_plot, nrow),
  duration = sapply(by_plot, function(p) max(p$Time)),
  early = sapply(by_plot, function(p) mean(p$Rate[p$Time <= 5])),
  late = sapply(by_plot, function(p) mean(tail(p$Rate, 5))),
  depth_30 = sapply(by_plot,
                    function(p) approx(c(0, p$Time), c(0, p$Depth), xout = 30)$y)
)
plot_summary$late_to_early = plot_summary$late / plot_summary$early
knitr::kable(plot_summary[order(plot_summary$erosion), ], digits = 3)
```

The summaries are positive and skewed, so we summarise each class by geometric means:

```{r}
geometric_means = sapply(
  plot_summary[, c("early", "late", "late_to_early", "depth_30")],
  function(x) tapply(x, plot_summary$erosion, function(v) exp(mean(log(v))))
)
round(geometric_means, 3)
```

@fig-summaries shows the same summaries with one point per plot, on a log scale.

```{r}
#| label: fig-summaries
#| fig-cap: "Summaries of each plot by degradation class (log scale): mean rate in the first
#|   5 minutes, mean of the last five readings, their ratio and the depth infiltrated in
#|   the first 30 minutes."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
summary_labels = c(early = "Early rate (cm/min)", late = "Late rate (cm/min)",
                   late_to_early = "Late / early rate",
                   depth_30 = "Depth in 30 min (cm)")
for (s in names(summary_labels)) {
  stripchart(plot_summary[[s]] ~ plot_summary$erosion, vertical = TRUE, log = "y",
             method = "jitter", jitter = 0.1, pch = erosion_symbols,
             col = erosion_colours, xlab = "Degradation class",
             ylab = summary_labels[[s]])
}
par(old_par)
```

This is the most useful figure for the research question. Within every class the plots
spread over a factor of about ten (depth in 30 minutes from
`r f1(min(plot_summary$depth_30))` to `r round(max(plot_summary$depth_30))` cm), and the
classes overlap almost completely. The geometric means of the depth in 30 minutes are
`r f1(geometric_means["E0", "depth_30"])` cm (E0),
`r f1(geometric_means["E1", "depth_30"])` cm (E1) and
`r f1(geometric_means["E2", "depth_30"])` cm (E2), differences that are small compared with
the spread among plots. The ratio of late to early rate, which describes the shape of the
decline and not its level, differs more consistently:
`r f2(geometric_means["E0", "late_to_early"])` in E0,
`r f2(geometric_means["E1", "late_to_early"])` in E1 and
`r f2(geometric_means["E2", "late_to_early"])` in E2. The E0 plots lose a larger fraction of
their early rate. @sec-candidates returns to this distinction between level and shape,
which turns out to matter for the model.

Did the runs stop when the rate had levelled off, and does that differ between classes?
@fig-duration plots the length of each run against its late rate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-duration
#| fig-cap: "Duration of each run against its late rate (log scale)."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
plot(duration ~ late, data = plot_summary, log = "x",
     col = erosion_colours[factor(plot_summary$erosion)],
     pch = erosion_symbols[factor(plot_summary$erosion)],
     xlab = "Late rate (cm/min)", ylab = "Duration of the run (min)")
legend("topright", legend = levels(infil$Erosion), col = erosion_colours,
       pch = erosion_symbols, bty = "n")
```

There is no clear relation between the duration of a run and its late rate or class, so
the different lengths of the runs do not seem to depend on the outcome. Neither the paper
nor the dissertation says when a run was stopped.

## The spread of the readings {#sec-spread}

Within each plot, the last ten readings vary around a nearly constant rate. Their standard
deviation against their mean (@fig-spread) shows how the spread depends on the rate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spread
#| fig-cap: "Standard deviation against mean of the last ten readings of each plot
#|   (log scales)."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
late_mean = sapply(by_plot, function(p) mean(tail(p$Rate, 10)))
late_sd = sapply(by_plot, function(p) sd(tail(p$Rate, 10)))
plot(late_sd ~ late_mean, log = "xy",
     col = erosion_colours[factor(plot_summary$erosion)],
     pch = erosion_symbols[factor(plot_summary$erosion)],
     xlab = "Mean of the last ten readings (cm/min)",
     ylab = "Standard deviation (cm/min)")
late_cv = late_sd / late_mean
summary(late_cv)
```

On log axes the points follow a line of slope about one: the standard deviation grows in
proportion to the mean, with a median coefficient of variation of `r f2(median(late_cv))`
(half of the plots between `r f2(quantile(late_cv, 0.25))` and
`r f2(quantile(late_cv, 0.75))`). A Normal distribution with a constant standard deviation
would be a poor model; the Gamma and LogNormal distributions with a constant coefficient
of variation, as in Case study 2, are the natural candidates. (This is also why the paper
fits `log(Rate)`.)

## What we take forward {#sec-forward}

- **The curve:** a fall that levels off, Horton or Philip (the paper's equations).
- **The readings:** positive, with a roughly constant coefficient of variation: Gamma or
  LogNormal with a mean and a coefficient of variation.
- **The groups:** the readings of a plot share its curve; plots differ by a factor of ten
  with roughly parallel curves on the log scale, so a random effect that multiplies the
  whole curve (alternative: one that multiplies the steady rate $f_c$ only).
- **The predictor:** the degradation class, a property of the plot, enters as a fixed effect
  through model matrices built from one row per plot (Chapter 7, `sec-model-matrix`).
- **Not modelled:** the early rises (@sec-no-first checks them), the resolution of the
  readings, and the similarity of successive readings (@sec-serial).

# The model {#sec-model}

## Curves and cumulative depths

Besides the rates, we need the cumulative depth of each curve, its integral from 0 to $t$:

$$
\text{Horton: } D(t) = f_c\,t + \frac{b}{k}\left(1 - e^{-kt}\right),
\qquad
\text{Philip: } D(t) = f_c\,t + S\sqrt{t}.
$$

We write Horton's curve with $b = f_0 - f_c$, the excess of the initial rate over the steady
rate (cm/min), which keeps $f_0$ above $f_c$ when both $f_c$ and $b$ are estimated on the
log scale. In the code, `b` is $f_0 - f_c$ for Horton and the sorptivity $S$ for Philip.

```{r}
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

horton_rate = function(t, fc, b, k) fc + b * exp(-k * t)
horton_depth = function(t, fc, b, k) fc * t + b * (1 - exp(-k * t)) / k
philip_rate = function(t, fc, b) fc + 0.5 * b / sqrt(t)
philip_depth = function(t, fc, b) fc * t + b * sqrt(t)
```

## The model for the readings

The model for reading $i$ of plot $j$, with the Horton curve, LogNormal readings and the
random effect on the whole curve, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(f_{c,j}) &= \beta_{c,0} + \beta_{c,1}\,C_{1j} + \beta_{c,2}\,C_{2j} + u_j,\\
\log(b_j) &= \beta_{b,0} + \beta_{b,1}\,C_{1j} + \beta_{b,2}\,C_{2j} + u_j,\\
u_j &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{plot}}),\\
\mu_{ij} &= f_{c,j} + b_j\,e^{-k t_{ij}},\\
R_{ij} \mid u_j &\sim \operatorname{LogNormal}\text{ with mean } \mu_{ij}
  \text{ and coefficient of variation } v,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_{1j}$ and $C_{2j}$ are 1 if plot $j$ is in class E1 or E2 and 0 otherwise,
$t_{ij}$ is the time of the reading and the readings are independent for given $u_j$. The
LogNormal distribution with mean $\mu$ and coefficient of variation $v$ has
$\sigma_{\log} = \sqrt{\log(1 + v^2)}$ and $\mu_{\log} = \log(\mu) - \sigma^2_{\log}/2$.

The same $u_j$ in the first two lines multiplies the whole curve of plot $j$ by
$e^{u_j}$. The typical curve of a class ($u_j = 0$) is that of its median plot, not of its
mean plot, which lies a factor $e^{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{plot}}/2}$ higher at every time;
ratios between classes are the same for both. The answer is the typical depth infiltrated
in the first 30 minutes in each class, $D(30)$ with $u_j = 0$, and the ratios E1/E0 and
E2/E0 of these depths.

## Implementation

The NLL needs the index of the plot of each reading (1 to 30), the degradation class of each
plot (`plot_info`, one row per plot, for the model matrices of the plots) and the three
classes (`classes`, one row per class, for the typical values). The list of data holds the
readings, the start and end of each interval, the plot index and the time over which we
compare the classes (min).

```{r}
plot_names = levels(infil$PlotNo)
plot_index = as.numeric(infil$PlotNo)
first_row = match(seq_along(plot_names), plot_index)
plot_info = infil[first_row, "Erosion", drop = FALSE]
classes = data.frame(Erosion = factor(levels(infil$Erosion),
                                      levels = levels(infil$Erosion)))
rownames(classes) = levels(infil$Erosion)

infil_data = list(rate = infil$Rate, t_start = infil$Start, t_end = infil$Time,
                  plot = plot_index, depth_time = 30)
```

One joint NLL covers every model of this document. Four choices are elements of the list
of data:

- `curve`: `"Horton"` or `"Philip"`;
- `distribution`: `"Gamma"` or `"LogNormal"`, both with a constant coefficient of
  variation;
- `random_on`: `"steady"` (the random effect multiplies $f_c$ only) or `"curve"` (it
  multiplies $f_c$ and $b$, so the whole curve of a plot is a constant factor higher or
  lower);
- `interval_mean`: `FALSE` compares a reading with the rate at the end of its interval,
  `TRUE` with the mean rate over the interval (the change in depth divided by its length),
  which is what a reading is (@sec-reading).

`ADREPORT()` gives the log of the typical depth in the first 30 minutes of each class and
the log ratios E1/E0 and E2/E0.

```{r}
infil_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  rate = OBS(rate)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the plots, before they are used.
  sd_plot = exp(log_sd_plot)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_plot, log = TRUE))
  # Parameters of each plot and typical parameters (u = 0) of each class.
  fc_plot = exp(X_fc %*% beta_fc + u)
  if (random_on == "curve") {
    b_plot = exp(X_b %*% beta_b + u)
  } else {
    b_plot = exp(X_b %*% beta_b)
  }
  fc_class = exp(X_fc_class %*% beta_fc)
  b_class = exp(X_b_class %*% beta_b)
  fc_i = fc_plot[plot]
  b_i = b_plot[plot]
  # Expected reading and typical depth in the first 30 minutes.
  if (curve == "Horton") {
    k_plot = exp(X_k %*% beta_k)
    k_i = k_plot[plot]
    if (interval_mean) {
      mu = (horton_depth(t_end, fc_i, b_i, k_i) -
              horton_depth(t_start, fc_i, b_i, k_i)) / (t_end - t_start)
    } else {
      mu = horton_rate(t_end, fc_i, b_i, k_i)
    }
    depth_class = horton_depth(depth_time, fc_class, b_class,
                               exp(X_k_class %*% beta_k))
  } else {
    if (interval_mean) {
      mu = (philip_depth(t_end, fc_i, b_i) - philip_depth(t_start, fc_i, b_i)) /
        (t_end - t_start)
    } else {
      mu = philip_rate(t_end, fc_i, b_i)
    }
    depth_class = philip_depth(depth_time, fc_class, b_class)
  }
  log_depth = log(depth_class)
  log_depth_ratio = log_depth[2:3] - log_depth[1]
  ADREPORT(log_depth)
  ADREPORT(log_depth_ratio)
  # Minus the log density of the readings for given deviations.
  cv = exp(log_cv)
  if (distribution == "Gamma") {
    nll = nll - sum(dgamma2(x = rate, mean = mu, sd = cv * mu, log = TRUE))
  } else {
    sdlog = sqrt(log(1 + cv^2))
    nll = nll - sum(dlnorm(x = rate, meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2,
                           sdlog = sdlog, log = TRUE))
  }
  nll
}
```

`infil_setup()` builds the list of data and the starting values for a list of formulas
(for $f_c$, $b$ and $k$), a curve, a distribution, the placement of the random effect and
the type of mean. The baseline values come from @sec-eda: late rates around 0.2 cm/min,
rates around 1 cm/min after a minute and most of the decline within 20 to 30 minutes ($k$
about 0.1/min); for Philip, $f_c + S/2 = 1$ at one minute gives $S$ about 1.8 cm/min^0.5^
with $f_c = 0.1$ cm/min. Every effect starts at zero, the coefficient of variation at 0.3
(@sec-spread) and the standard deviation among plots at 0.5. Every fit in this document
converged from these values. The formula for $k$ is ignored for Philip.

```{r}
infil_setup = function(data, plot_info, classes, formulas, curve, distribution,
                       random_on, interval_mean = FALSE) {
  data$curve = curve
  data$distribution = distribution
  data$random_on = random_on
  data$interval_mean = interval_mean
  data$X_fc = model.matrix(formulas$fc, data = plot_info)
  data$X_b = model.matrix(formulas$b, data = plot_info)
  data$X_fc_class = model.matrix(formulas$fc, data = classes)
  data$X_b_class = model.matrix(formulas$b, data = classes)
  if (curve == "Horton") {
    baseline = c(fc = 0.2, b = 0.8, k = 0.1)
  } else {
    baseline = c(fc = 0.1, b = 1.8)
  }
  start = list(
    beta_fc = c(log(baseline[["fc"]]), rep(0, ncol(data$X_fc) - 1)),
    beta_b = c(log(baseline[["b"]]), rep(0, ncol(data$X_b) - 1)),
    log_cv = log(0.3),
    log_sd_plot = log(0.5)
  )
  if (curve == "Horton") {
    data$X_k = model.matrix(formulas$k, data = plot_info)
    data$X_k_class = model.matrix(formulas$k, data = classes)
    start$beta_k = c(log(baseline[["k"]]), rep(0, ncol(data$X_k) - 1))
  }
  list(data = data, start = start)
}
```

Three helpers complete the toolkit:

- `fit_infil()` processes the joint NLL for one list of data, integrating out `u`, and
  minimises it;
- `aic_table()` reports, for a named list of fits, $K$, the log-likelihood, the
  convergence code, the largest absolute gradient at the solution, AIC and the difference
  from the lowest AIC;
- `depth_answer()` gives the typical depth in 30 minutes per class (cm) and the ratios
  E1/E0 and E2/E0, with Wald intervals calculated on the log scale and transformed back.

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

fit_infil = function(data, start) {
  start$u = rep(0, max(data$plot))
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(infil_nll, data), start, random = "u", silent = TRUE)
  fit = optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  list(obj = obj, fit = fit)
}

aic_table = function(fits) {
  out = data.frame(
    model = names(fits),
    K = sapply(fits, function(f) length(f$fit$par)),
    loglik = sapply(fits, function(f) -f$fit$value),
    convergence = sapply(fits, function(f) f$fit$convergence),
    max_gradient = sapply(fits, function(f) max(abs(f$obj$gr(f$fit$par))))
  )
  out$aic = 2 * out$K - 2 * out$loglik
  out$delta_aic = out$aic - min(out$aic)
  rownames(out) = NULL
  out
}

critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
depth_answer = function(obj) {
  report = summary(sdreport(obj), select = "report")
  data.frame(
    quantity = c("depth E0", "depth E1", "depth E2", "ratio E1/E0", "ratio E2/E0"),
    estimate = exp(report[, "Estimate"]),
    lower = exp(report[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * report[, "Std. Error"]),
    upper = exp(report[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * report[, "Std. Error"])
  )
}

# Print an AIC table or an answer table in the document.
show_table = function(tab, digits = 2) {
  if ("max_gradient" %in% names(tab)) {
    tab$max_gradient = format(signif(tab$max_gradient, 2))
  }
  knitr::kable(tab, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

# Which curve, which distribution, which random effect? {#sec-choices}

The full model lets the degradation class change every parameter of the curve, so that the
comparison is not affected by effects that we left out (as in Case study 2). Two curves,
two distributions and two placements of the random effect make eight fits.

```{r}
full_formulas = list(fc = ~ Erosion, b = ~ Erosion, k = ~ Erosion)

choices = expand.grid(curve = c("Horton", "Philip"),
                      distribution = c("Gamma", "LogNormal"),
                      random_on = c("steady", "curve"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
choice_fits = list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(choices))) {
  setup = infil_setup(infil_data, plot_info, classes, full_formulas,
                      choices$curve[i], choices$distribution[i],
                      choices$random_on[i])
  choice_fits[[i]] = fit_infil(setup$data, setup$start)
}
names(choice_fits) = paste(choices$curve, choices$distribution, choices$random_on)
choice_table = aic_table(choice_fits)
show_table(choice_table[order(choice_table$aic), ], digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# AIC differences quoted in the text.
aic_choice = setNames(choice_table$aic, choice_table$model)
re_gap = aic_choice[1:4] - aic_choice[5:8]
gamma_gap_philip = aic_choice[["Philip Gamma curve"]] -
  aic_choice[["Philip LogNormal curve"]]
gamma_gap_horton = aic_choice[["Horton Gamma curve"]] -
  aic_choice[["Horton LogNormal curve"]]
philip_gap = aic_choice[["Horton LogNormal curve"]] -
  aic_choice[["Philip LogNormal curve"]]
```

`r if (all(choice_table$convergence == 0)) "All eight fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The placement of the random effect matters most: a random effect on the whole curve beats
one on $f_c$ only by `r round(min(re_gap))` to `r round(max(re_gap))` AIC units for every
curve and distribution, as the parallel curves of @fig-curves suggested. With the random
effect on the whole curve, LogNormal beats Gamma (by `r round(gamma_gap_philip)` units for
Philip, `r round(gamma_gap_horton)` for Horton), and Philip beats Horton (by
`r f1(philip_gap)` units with LogNormal readings).

We nevertheless continue with Horton and LogNormal, and use Philip as a check in
@sec-philip, for a reason that only shows there: with effects of the class on $f_c$,
Philip's steady rate of E0 runs off to zero (log($f_c$) near −10 with a standard error of
40), an estimate at the boundary that is Chapter 8 material. Horton's parameters all stay
inside their range, and the answer is the same with both curves. Horton's fit is also the
more useful one for students, because $f_0$, $f_c$ and $k$ can be read from the figures of
@sec-eda as starting values, and the curve is the falling exponential of the functions
supplement with an offset.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Follow the AIC and use Philip, discuss the boundary estimate of $f_c$ for E0, and answer
with the depth in 30 minutes, which the boundary does not affect.
:::

# Which parameters depend on the degradation class? {#sec-candidates}

With the Horton curve, LogNormal readings and a random effect on the whole curve, the
candidates have no effect of the class (`none`), an effect on $f_c$ only (`steady`), on
$b = f_0 - f_c$ only (`excess`), on both (`both`), and on all three parameters (`full`).

```{r}
candidates = list(
  none = list(fc = ~ 1, b = ~ 1, k = ~ 1),
  steady = list(fc = ~ Erosion, b = ~ 1, k = ~ 1),
  excess = list(fc = ~ 1, b = ~ Erosion, k = ~ 1),
  both = list(fc = ~ Erosion, b = ~ Erosion, k = ~ 1),
  full = full_formulas
)
candidate_setups = list()
candidate_fits = list()
for (m in names(candidates)) {
  candidate_setups[[m]] = infil_setup(infil_data, plot_info, classes, candidates[[m]],
                                      "Horton", "LogNormal", "curve")
  candidate_fits[[m]] = fit_infil(candidate_setups[[m]]$data,
                                  candidate_setups[[m]]$start)
}
candidate_table = aic_table(candidate_fits)
show_table(candidate_table, digits = 1)
```

The typical depth in 30 minutes per class (rows) under each candidate (columns):

```{r}
candidate_depths = sapply(candidate_fits,
                          function(f) depth_answer(f$obj)$estimate[1:3])
rownames(candidate_depths) = rownames(classes)
round(candidate_depths, 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
delta_cand = setNames(candidate_table$delta_aic, candidate_table$model)
```

`r if (all(candidate_table$convergence == 0)) "All five fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The candidate `none` is worse than the best by `r f1(delta_cand[["none"]])` AIC units, so
the classes differ in some way. `steady` and `excess` are tied
(`r f1(abs(delta_cand[["steady"]] - delta_cand[["excess"]]))` units apart), and `both` and
`full` are `r f1(delta_cand[["both"]])` and `r f1(delta_cand[["full"]])` units behind the
best.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: two tied candidates give opposite answers"}
Under `steady` the typical E0 plot takes up the least water in 30 minutes
(`r f1(candidate_depths["E0", "steady"])` cm against
`r f1(candidate_depths["E1", "steady"])` cm in E1), under `excess` the most
(`r f1(candidate_depths["E0", "excess"])` against
`r f1(candidate_depths["E1", "excess"])` cm).

The reason is the random effect on the whole curve. It already gives every plot its own
level, so an effect of the class on one parameter changes mainly the shape of the curve
(the ratio of $f_c$ to $f_0 - f_c$: in E0 the rate falls further from its start,
@sec-plot-summaries), and the level of each class then follows from the parameter that the
formula happens to name. Both candidates describe the same shape difference equally well,
which is why their AIC is the same, and neither has a free parameter for the level.

A question about the level needs a model in which the class can change the level and the
shape separately: `both`. Its typical depths (`r f1(candidate_depths["E0", "both"])`,
`r f1(candidate_depths["E1", "both"])` and `r f1(candidate_depths["E2", "both"])` cm) are
close to the geometric means of the plots in @sec-plot-summaries
(`r f1(geometric_means["E0", "depth_30"])`, `r f1(geometric_means["E1", "depth_30"])` and
`r f1(geometric_means["E2", "depth_30"])` cm), which those of `steady` and `excess` are
not.
:::

**Teaching point.** AIC ranks the candidates as descriptions of the data; it does not tell
which candidate can answer the question. The question decides that the level must be free,
and AIC then shows that the extra freedom costs little (`r f1(delta_cand[["both"]])`
units).

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative: a level-shape parameterisation"}
Reparameterise the curve as level times shape, for example
$f(t) = r_{30}\left(p + (1 - p)\,e^{-k(t - 30)}\right)$, with $r_{30}$ the rate at 30
minutes and $p = f_c/r_{30}$, and put the class effects on $\log(r_{30})$ and
$\operatorname{logit}(p)$. This makes the level a parameter. In a quick trial (not part of
this document) it reproduced the same AIC pattern, but the Horton version stopped at a
false optimum from simple starting values, and Philip's $p$ for E0 again went to the
boundary, so it is not used here.
:::

# The answer: how much water do the classes take up? {#sec-answer}

We take the candidate `both` and calculate its `sdreport()`.

```{r}
both_data = candidate_setups$both$data
both_start = candidate_setups$both$start
both = candidate_fits$both
both_obj = both$obj
both_fit = both$fit
both_fit$convergence
both_sd = sdreport(both_obj)
```

The typical depth in the first 30 minutes per class and the ratios, with Wald intervals:

```{r}
both_answer = depth_answer(both_obj)
show_table(both_answer)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Estimate and interval of row r of an answer table, as text.
answer_text = function(tab, r) {
  paste0(f2(tab$estimate[r]), " (", f2(tab$lower[r]), " to ", f2(tab$upper[r]), ")")
}
```

The typical E0 plot takes up `r f1(both_answer$estimate[1])` cm of water in the first 30
minutes (95% interval `r f1(both_answer$lower[1])` to `r f1(both_answer$upper[1])` cm),
the typical E1 plot `r f1(both_answer$estimate[2])` cm (`r f1(both_answer$lower[2])` to
`r f1(both_answer$upper[2])`) and the typical E2 plot `r f1(both_answer$estimate[3])` cm
(`r f1(both_answer$lower[3])` to `r f1(both_answer$upper[3])`). The ratio E1/E0 is
`r answer_text(both_answer, 4)` and the ratio E2/E0 `r answer_text(both_answer, 5)`. The
data are compatible with no difference and with differences of a factor of two in either
direction. The reason is visible in @fig-summaries: the plots of a class differ by a
factor of ten, and there are only `r n_class[["E0"]]`, `r n_class[["E1"]]` and
`r n_class[["E2"]]` of them. The honest answer is that these 30 runs cannot tell whether
the degradation classes take up different amounts of water.

::: {.callout-note title="Comparison with the dissertation (for the author)"}
The dissertation fitted Philip's equation with `nlme` to all 180 plots, with the class as a
covariate of the fixed effects (Omuto 2006, Table 4.5). Both parameters decrease from E0 to
E2: steady rates of 0.47, 0.21 and 0.10 cm/min and sorptivities of 5.37, 2.48 and 1.23
cm/min^0.5^, reported as significantly different between classes (Table 4.6 gives the
steady rate in cm/hour, so its unit is uncertain). With six times as many plots, 47 of
them in E2, the classes separate clearly there. These data cannot tell whether the
difference from our answer comes from the smaller sample, from the selection of the 30
plots or from the model (Philip with errors of constant standard deviation on the rate
there; a plot effect on the whole curve and LogNormal readings here). The dissertation's
result should not be given to students before they analyse the data.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: narrow intervals from a model that fixes the ratio"}
A student who reports the `steady` or `excess` model, the best by AIC, gets narrow
intervals for a ratio that the model fixes by its formula (in the trial with the
level-shape parameterisation, the "shape only" model gave standard errors of 0.02 to 0.05
on the log scale, against
`r f2(summary(both_sd, select = "report")[4, "Std. Error"])` and
`r f2(summary(both_sd, select = "report")[5, "Std. Error"])` here).
:::

The estimates on the optimised scales, labelled by parameter and column of the model
matrix:

```{r}
both_fixed = summary(both_sd, select = "fixed")
rownames(both_fixed) = c(paste0("fc_", colnames(both_data$X_fc)),
                         paste0("b_", colnames(both_data$X_b)),
                         "log_cv", "log_sd_plot", "log_k")
round(both_fixed, 3)
```

The typical parameters of the classes on the original scale, $f_c$ and $f_0 = f_c + b$
(cm/min) and $k$ (1/min):

```{r}
both_par = split(both_fit$par, names(both_fit$par))
class_parameters = data.frame(
  fc = exp(both_data$X_fc_class %*% both_par$beta_fc),
  f0 = exp(both_data$X_fc_class %*% both_par$beta_fc) +
    exp(both_data$X_b_class %*% both_par$beta_b),
  k = exp(both_par$beta_k),
  row.names = rownames(classes)
)
round(class_parameters, 3)
```

The typical steady rates are `r f2(class_parameters$fc[1])` (E0),
`r f2(class_parameters$fc[2])` (E1) and `r f2(class_parameters$fc[3])` cm/min (E2), and
the typical initial rates `r f2(class_parameters$f0[1])`, `r f2(class_parameters$f0[2])`
and `r f2(class_parameters$f0[3])` cm/min. The decay rate is
`r f2(class_parameters$k[1])`/min, so the excess $f_0 - f_c$ falls to a tenth of its
initial value after about `r round(log(10) / class_parameters$k[1])` minutes
($\log(10)/k$). Every effect of a class has a standard error of
`r f2(min(both_fixed[c(2, 3, 5, 6), "Std. Error"]))` to
`r f2(max(both_fixed[c(2, 3, 5, 6), "Std. Error"]))` on the log scale, as large as or
larger than the effect itself.

The coefficient of variation of the readings, and the standard deviation among plots with
a likelihood profile interval (calculated on the log scale and transformed back):

```{r}
cv_both = exp(both_fit$par[["log_cv"]])
cv_both
both_profile_sd = TMB::tmbprofile(both_obj, name = "log_sd_plot", trace = FALSE)
sd_plot_ci = exp(c(estimate = both_fit$par[["log_sd_plot"]],
                   confint(both_profile_sd)[1, ]))
sd_plot_ci
```

The readings vary around the curve of their plot with a coefficient of variation of
`r f2(cv_both)`, more than the median of `r f2(median(late_cv))` among the late readings in
@sec-spread; the early readings may vary more, and the shape of some plots differs from
the typical curve (@sec-two-re). The standard deviation among plots is
`r f2(sd_plot_ci[1])` on the log scale (profile interval `r f2(sd_plot_ci[2])` to
`r f2(sd_plot_ci[3])`): the middle 95% of plots of a class span a factor of
$e^{2 \times 1.96 \times `r f2(sd_plot_ci[1])`}$, about
`r round(exp(2 * critical_value * sd_plot_ci[1]))`. This variation, not the readings,
limits the answer.

@fig-typical shows the typical curves of the three classes over the readings.

```{r}
#| label: fig-typical
#| fig-cap: "Readings (points) and typical curves (u = 0) of the three degradation classes
#|   under the model `both`, on the log scale."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.9
time_grid = seq(from = 0.5, to = 90, length.out = 300)
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (e in 1:3) {
  infil_class = infil[infil$Erosion == levels(infil$Erosion)[e], ]
  plot(Rate ~ Time, data = infil_class, log = "y", ylim = range(infil$Rate),
       col = erosion_colours[e], pch = erosion_symbols[e], cex = 0.7,
       main = levels(infil$Erosion)[e], xlab = "Time (min)",
       ylab = "Infiltration rate (cm/min)")
  lines(time_grid, horton_rate(time_grid, class_parameters$fc[e],
                               class_parameters$f0[e] - class_parameters$fc[e],
                               class_parameters$k[e]), lwd = 2)
}
par(old_par)
```

The typical curves run through the middle of the readings on the log scale (they are the
curves of the median plot). The horizontal bands of points at 0.05, 0.1, 0.15 and
0.2 cm/min are the resolution of the readings (@sec-reading).

# Checking the model {#sec-checks}

## Scaled quantile residuals {#sec-residuals}

We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples (new plot deviations, then new readings for them)
and compare each reading with the typical curve of its class at the time of the reading.

```{r}
n_sim = 1000
infil_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(both_data$rate), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 2009)
for (s in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  infil_simulations[, s] = both_obj$simulate(both_fit$par)$rate
}

class_of_reading = as.numeric(infil$Erosion)
infil_expected = horton_rate(infil$Time, class_parameters$fc[class_of_reading],
                             class_parameters$f0[class_of_reading] -
                               class_parameters$fc[class_of_reading],
                             class_parameters$k[class_of_reading])

infil_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = infil_simulations,
  observedResponse = both_data$rate,
  fittedPredictedResponse = infil_expected
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the model `both`: quantile-quantile plot (left)
#|   and residuals against the predicted rate (right)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
plot(infil_residuals)
dispersion_rate = DHARMa::testDispersion(infil_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
dispersion_rate
```

The quantile-quantile plot is close to the line but slightly S-shaped. In the right panel
the quartiles of the residuals lie a little above their expected values over most of the
range, and below them at the lowest predictions (late readings of the class curves with
the lowest steady rates), where the median residual drops to about 0.4. The dispersion
statistic is `r f2(dispersion_rate)`: the readings vary around the typical curves about
half as much (as a variance, on the scale of the rates) as in the simulated samples. As in
Chapter 6, the p-values that DHARMa prints on its plots are not used for decisions: with
1,105 readings a small p-value does not say how much the disagreement matters.

The dispersion statistic works on the scale of the rates, where the plots with the highest
simulated rates dominate the simulated variance. The same comparison on the log scale,
where the model is LogNormal at both levels:

```{r}
log_deviation = log(both_data$rate) - log(infil_expected)
log_simulated = log(infil_simulations) - log(infil_expected)
dispersion_log = var(log_deviation) / mean(apply(log_simulated, 2, var))
dispersion_log
```

On the log scale the ratio is `r f2(dispersion_log)`: the readings vary around the typical
curves about as much as the model expects. The low statistic on the scale of the rates
mostly reflects the long right tail of the simulated plots (a plot two standard deviations
above the typical one is $e^{2 \times `r f2(sd_plot_ci[1])`}$, about
`r f1(exp(2 * sd_plot_ci[1]))` times faster at every time), which dominates the simulated
variance of the rates.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the dispersion statistic with a large variance among groups"}
With a LogNormal model and a large variance among groups, read DHARMa's dispersion
statistic with care; the quantile residuals themselves are unaffected.
:::

@fig-dharma-time shows the residuals against time and against the degradation class.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma-time
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals against time (left) and degradation class (right)."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
DHARMa::plotResiduals(infil_residuals, form = infil$Time)
DHARMa::plotResiduals(infil_residuals, form = infil$Erosion)
par(old_par)
```

Against time, the median residual is a little above 0.5 at the start and the lower
quartile drifts from about 0.35 to 0.25: early in a run the readings are higher than the
model expects more often than late in a run. The classes look similar.

One residual per plot, from the sum of its readings:

```{r}
plot_residuals = DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(infil_residuals, group = both_data$plot)
plot_scaled = residuals(plot_residuals)
names(plot_scaled) = plot_names
round(sort(plot_scaled), 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lowest_plots = names(sort(plot_scaled))[1:3]
```

The residuals of the plots spread over the whole range, from
`r f2(min(plot_scaled))` (`r names(which.min(plot_scaled))`) to
`r f2(max(plot_scaled))` (`r names(which.max(plot_scaled))`). The three lowest
(`r paste(lowest_plots, collapse = ", ")`, all below
`r f2(ceiling(100 * max(sort(plot_scaled)[1:3])) / 100)`) are the three plots with the
lowest late rates (`r f2(min(plot_summary[lowest_plots, "late"]))` to
`r f2(max(plot_summary[lowest_plots, "late"]))` cm/min), and
`r names(which.max(plot_scaled))` has the highest. Among 30 plots, three below 0.06 is a
little more than expected (about two), but not a clear disagreement: the Normal
distribution of the plot deviations covers the range of plots.

## Successive readings of the same plot {#sec-serial}

The residuals above come from new plot deviations, so the readings of one plot share their
deviation. Removing the mean of each plot (on the Normal scale) leaves the variation within
plots; the correlation of each residual with the next one of the same plot measures how
much successive readings resemble each other.

```{r}
next_same_plot = c(infil$PlotNo[-1] == infil$PlotNo[-nrow(infil)], FALSE)
normal_residuals = qnorm(pmin(pmax(residuals(infil_residuals), 0.001), 0.999))
within_plot = normal_residuals - ave(normal_residuals, infil$PlotNo)
serial_cor = cor(within_plot[next_same_plot], within_plot[which(next_same_plot) + 1])
serial_cor
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: correlated successive readings"}
The correlation is `r f2(serial_cor)`. Successive readings of a run are not independent
for a given plot deviation, as the model assumes: a reading above the curve tends to be
followed by another (the curve of a plot also differs in shape from the typical one,
@sec-two-re). Within-plot quantities ($k$ and the coefficient of variation) therefore have
standard errors that are too small. The comparison of the classes rests mainly on the
variation among plots, which the model represents, so it is less affected. The course has
no tools for serial correlation, and the simulation of @sec-simulation cannot reveal its
effect, because it simulates from the model without it. Students can be asked to calculate
this correlation and discuss it.
:::

## Rate at the end or mean rate over the interval? {#sec-interval-mean}

A reading is the mean rate over its interval (@sec-reading), so the expected reading is
the change in depth over the interval divided by its length.

```{r}
interval_setup = infil_setup(infil_data, plot_info, classes, candidates$both,
                             "Horton", "LogNormal", "curve", interval_mean = TRUE)
interval_fit = fit_infil(interval_setup$data, interval_setup$start)
interval_table = aic_table(list(end_rate = both, interval_mean = interval_fit))
show_table(interval_table, digits = 1)
interval_answer = depth_answer(interval_fit$obj)
```

The interval mean is better by `r f1(interval_table$aic[1] - interval_table$aic[2])` AIC
units (same $K$), a small difference, because the curve changes slowly within one or two
minutes except at the very start. The answer changes little (table in @sec-philip).

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Use the interval mean in the main model. It is what the falling-head method measures, so
it is the more faithful choice; it needs the cumulative depth function, which students can
derive by integrating the rate (a good exercise).
:::

## Without the first reading of each plot {#sec-no-first}

`subset_rows()` keeps only the given readings (the plots do not change). We refit `both`
without the first reading of each plot, which removes most of the early rises of
@sec-rises.

```{r}
subset_rows = function(data, rows) {
  data$rate = data$rate[rows]
  data$t_start = data$t_start[rows]
  data$t_end = data$t_end[rows]
  data$plot = data$plot[rows]
  data
}
not_first = !(seq_len(nrow(infil)) %in% first_row)
no_first_fit = fit_infil(subset_rows(both_data, not_first), both_start)
no_first_fit$fit$convergence
no_first_answer = depth_answer(no_first_fit$obj)
```

The answer changes little (table in @sec-philip).

## Philip's curve {#sec-philip}

```{r}
philip_setup = infil_setup(infil_data, plot_info, classes, candidates$both, "Philip",
                           "LogNormal", "curve")
philip_fit = fit_infil(philip_setup$data, philip_setup$start)
philip_table = aic_table(list(horton = both, philip = philip_fit))
show_table(philip_table, digits = 1)
philip_answer = depth_answer(philip_fit$obj)
philip_fixed = summary(sdreport(philip_fit$obj), select = "fixed")
rownames(philip_fixed) = c(paste0("fc_", colnames(philip_setup$data$X_fc)),
                           paste0("S_", colnames(philip_setup$data$X_b)),
                           "log_cv", "log_sd_plot")
round(philip_fixed, 3)
```

Philip is better by `r f1(philip_table$aic[1] - philip_table$aic[2])` AIC units with one
parameter fewer.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: an estimate at the boundary with a converged fit"}
Philip's steady rate of E0 is at the boundary: log($f_c$) of E0 is
`r f2(philip_fixed["fc_(Intercept)", "Estimate"])` ($f_c$ practically zero) with a standard
error of `r f1(philip_fixed["fc_(Intercept)", "Std. Error"])`, and the effects of E1 and E2
on log($f_c$) are just as large and uncertain. The optimiser reports convergence; only the
estimates and standard errors show the problem. For E0 the Philip curve explains the whole
decline by sorptivity, with no steady component. Likelihood profiles and Wald intervals of
these coefficients are meaningless, but the depth in 30 minutes is unaffected. With all
180 plots, the dissertation estimated the steady rate of E0 at 0.47 cm/min, the highest of
the three classes (@sec-answer), so the boundary comes from these 30 plots and this model.
:::

The answer under the four variants of this section:

```{r}
sensitivity = data.frame(
  quantity = both_answer$quantity,
  main = both_answer$estimate,
  interval_mean = interval_answer$estimate,
  without_first = no_first_answer$estimate,
  philip = philip_answer$estimate
)
show_table(sensitivity)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
ratio_range_1 = range(unlist(sensitivity[4, -1]))
ratio_range_2 = range(unlist(sensitivity[5, -1]))
philip_shift = range(sensitivity$philip[1:3] - sensitivity$main[1:3])
```

The ratios hardly move (E1/E0 from `r f2(ratio_range_1[1])` to `r f2(ratio_range_1[2])`,
E2/E0 from `r f2(ratio_range_2[1])` to `r f2(ratio_range_2[2])`), far less than their
intervals. Philip's typical depths are `r f1(philip_shift[1])` to
`r f1(philip_shift[2])` cm higher in every class: the curves differ in the first minutes,
where Philip's rate is infinite. Like the asymptotes in Case study 2, parameters beyond the
data ($f_c$ as $t$ grows, $f_0$ at $t = 0$) depend on the curve, and quantities inside the
data (ratios of depth in 30 minutes) do not.

# Beyond the course: two random effects per plot {#sec-two-re}

Chapter 7 uses one random effect per group. Here the plots get independent deviations of
$\log(f_c)$ ($u_j$, standard deviation $\sigma_{c}$) and of $\log(b)$ ($v_j$, standard
deviation $\sigma_{b}$), so that the shape of the curve can vary between plots too.

```{r}
infil_nll_2re = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  rate = OBS(rate)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_fc), log = TRUE))
  nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = v, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_b), log = TRUE))
  fc_plot = exp(X_fc %*% beta_fc + u)
  b_plot = exp(X_b %*% beta_b + v)
  k_plot = exp(X_k %*% beta_k)
  mu = horton_rate(t_end, fc_plot[plot], b_plot[plot], k_plot[plot])
  depth_class = horton_depth(depth_time, exp(X_fc_class %*% beta_fc),
                             exp(X_b_class %*% beta_b), exp(X_k_class %*% beta_k))
  log_depth = log(depth_class)
  log_depth_ratio = log_depth[2:3] - log_depth[1]
  ADREPORT(log_depth)
  ADREPORT(log_depth_ratio)
  sdlog = sqrt(log(1 + exp(log_cv)^2))
  nll - sum(dlnorm(x = rate, meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog = sdlog,
                   log = TRUE))
}
start_2re = both_start
start_2re$log_sd_plot = NULL
start_2re$log_sd_fc = log(0.5)
start_2re$log_sd_b = log(0.5)
start_2re$u = rep(0, length(plot_names))
start_2re$v = rep(0, length(plot_names))
obj_2re = MakeADFun(cmb(infil_nll_2re, both_data), start_2re,
                    random = c("u", "v"), silent = TRUE)
fit_2re = optim(par = obj_2re$par, fn = obj_2re$fn, gr = obj_2re$gr,
                method = "BFGS")
table_2re = aic_table(list(one_random_effect = both,
                           two_random_effects = list(obj = obj_2re, fit = fit_2re)))
show_table(table_2re, digits = 1)
sd_2re = exp(fit_2re$par[c("log_sd_fc", "log_sd_b")])
sd_2re
answer_2re = depth_answer(obj_2re)
show_table(answer_2re)
```

Two random effects are better by `r round(table_2re$aic[1] - table_2re$aic[2])` AIC units
with one parameter more: the plots differ in the shape of their decline, not only in its
level (standard deviations of `r f2(sd_2re[1])` for $\log(f_c)$ and `r f2(sd_2re[2])` for
$\log(f_0 - f_c)$). The answer is the same (ratios `r f2(answer_2re$estimate[4])` and
`r f2(answer_2re$estimate[5])`) with narrower intervals (`r f2(answer_2re$lower[4])` to
`r f2(answer_2re$upper[4])` and `r f2(answer_2re$lower[5])` to
`r f2(answer_2re$upper[5])`), which still include 1. Independent deviations are an
assumption; a correlation between them (as in the paper's `nlme` example for water
retention) is a further step beyond the course. This is the model a researcher would
probably prefer; for students the model with one random effect answers the question in the
same way.

# Checking the estimator by simulation {#sec-simulation}

We draw 300 hypothetical samples of 30 plots from the fitted model `both` (same plots,
classes and times) and fit each from the same starting values as the data. We keep the log
ratios of the typical depth (estimates and standard errors) and the standard deviation
among plots.

```{r}
set.seed(seed = 1940)
n_samples = 300
sim_log_ratio = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 2)
sim_se = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 2)
sim_sd_plot = rep(NA, n_samples)
n_failed = 0
for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
  sim_data = both_data
  sim_data$rate = both_obj$simulate(both_fit$par)$rate
  sim = fit_infil(sim_data, both_start)
  n_failed = n_failed + (sim$fit$convergence != 0)
  sim_report = summary(sdreport(sim$obj), select = "report")
  sim_log_ratio[i, ] = sim_report[4:5, "Estimate"]
  sim_se[i, ] = sim_report[4:5, "Std. Error"]
  sim_sd_plot[i] = exp(sim$fit$par[["log_sd_plot"]])
}
n_failed
```

The bias, the standard deviation of the estimates, the mean standard error and the
coverage of the 95% Wald interval for the log ratios E1/E0 (row 1) and E2/E0 (row 2):

```{r}
log_ratio_used = summary(both_sd, select = "report")[4:5, "Estimate"]
log_ratio_matrix = matrix(log_ratio_used, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
covered = abs(sim_log_ratio - log_ratio_matrix) < critical_value * sim_se
sim_summary = data.frame(
  ratio = c("E1/E0", "E2/E0"),
  bias = colMeans(sim_log_ratio) - log_ratio_used,
  sd_estimates = apply(sim_log_ratio, 2, sd),
  mean_se = colMeans(sim_se),
  coverage = colMeans(covered)
)
show_table(sim_summary, digits = 3)
```

`r if (n_failed == 0) "Every fit converged." else paste(n_failed, "fits did not converge.")`
The bias is small compared with the standard error
(`r formatC(sim_summary$bias[1], format = "f", digits = 3)` and
`r formatC(sim_summary$bias[2], format = "f", digits = 3)` against `r f2(sim_summary$mean_se[1])` and
`r f2(sim_summary$mean_se[2])`), the standard errors agree with the standard deviations of
the estimates, and the coverages, `r f1(100 * sim_summary$coverage[1])`% and
`r f1(100 * sim_summary$coverage[2])`%, are close to the range of about 92.5% to 97.5% that
300 samples give for a coverage of 95%. So with 30 plots the Wald intervals of the ratios
work, under the model; @sec-serial explains what this check cannot see.

The standard deviation among plots used to simulate, and the mean and median of its
estimates:

```{r}
sd_plot_check = c(simulated = exp(both_fit$par[["log_sd_plot"]]),
                  mean = mean(sim_sd_plot), median = median(sim_sd_plot))
sd_plot_check
```

The estimates of the standard deviation among plots are about
`r round(100 * (1 - sd_plot_check[["mean"]] / sd_plot_check[["simulated"]]))`% too small on
average (`r f2(sd_plot_check[["mean"]])` against `r f2(sd_plot_check[["simulated"]])`):
the bias of maximum likelihood variances (Chapter 7, REML). It does not matter for the
ratios.

# Summary: alternatives, pitfalls and teaching notes {#sec-summary}

**Answer.** The typical depth of water taken up in the first 30 minutes is
`r f1(both_answer$estimate[1])` cm (E0), `r f1(both_answer$estimate[2])` cm (E1) and
`r f1(both_answer$estimate[3])` cm (E2), with ratios E1/E0 = `r answer_text(both_answer, 4)`
and E2/E0 = `r answer_text(both_answer, 5)`. The classes differ in the shape of the decline
(E0 loses a larger fraction of its initial rate), but the 30 plots cannot tell whether
they differ in the amount of water they take up. The variation among plots of a class (a
factor of about `r round(exp(2 * critical_value * sd_plot_ci[1]))` for the middle 95%)
dwarfs any difference between classes. With all 180 plots of the survey, the dissertation
found clear differences between the classes (@sec-answer).

**Pitfalls.**

1. `Cumrate` is the running sum of the rates, not the cumulative depth (@sec-reading).
2. Readings are whole millimetres over 1 to 10 minutes: low rates take few values and the
   resolution is coarse (@sec-reading). The rates are means over intervals of unequal
   length (@sec-interval-mean).
3. `r sum(rises)` plots rise before they fall (@sec-rises); no curve of the paper can
   rise.
4. The information about the classes comes from 30 plots (`r n_class[["E0"]]`,
   `r n_class[["E1"]]` and `r n_class[["E2"]]`), not from 1,105 readings (@sec-design).
5. A random effect on $f_c$ only is much worse than one on the whole curve
   (@sec-choices).
6. With a random effect on the whole curve, a class effect on one parameter fixes the
   level difference by assumption: two candidates tie on AIC and give opposite answers
   (@sec-candidates). The question, not AIC alone, decides which effects must be in the
   model.
7. Philip's $f_c$ of E0 goes to the boundary with "converged" fits (@sec-philip; Chapter 8
   material).
8. Successive readings are correlated within plots (`r f2(serial_cor)`, @sec-serial); the
   course has no tool for this, and the simulation check cannot detect its effect.
9. The classes are visual classes of physical degradation (@sec-data), assigned by eye
   before the measurements; only E2 involves erosion, although the column is called
   `Erosion`. The class is an observed property of each plot, not a treatment, so
   differences between classes, if any, would not show that degradation causes them. The
   30 plots were selected from 180 in an undocumented way, E2 is under-represented, and
   plots may share a block (@sec-design).
10. The paper's own example fits Philip's equation to `log(Rate)` with `nls()` (Section
    3.1 of the paper), so its $f_c = -1.64$ is on the log scale
    ($e^{-1.64} \approx 0.19$ cm/min), which students may misread as a negative rate.

**Alternatives.**

- Philip's curve (lower AIC, boundary estimate; @sec-choices and @sec-philip).
- Gamma readings (worse by `r round(gamma_gap_philip)` to `r round(gamma_gap_horton)` AIC
  units; @sec-choices).
- Interval means instead of end rates (@sec-interval-mean).
- Without the first readings (@sec-no-first).
- Two independent random effects (@sec-two-re; beyond Chapter 7).
- A level-shape parameterisation (@sec-candidates; unstable here).
- Other answer quantities inside the data: the typical rate at 30 minutes, or the ratio of
  the rate at 30 minutes to the rate at 1 minute (a measure of shape, which is where the
  classes do differ). Both are one line of `ADREPORT()`.
- Fitting the cumulative depth instead of the rates is not recommended: successive depths
  share all earlier readings, so they are strongly dependent.

**Teaching notes (possible questions for students).**

- Show that rate × interval is a whole number of millimetres and explain what a reading is;
  calculate the cumulative depth correctly.
- Derive the depth function of each curve by integrating the rate.
- Read starting values for Horton from the figures ($f_c$ from the late rates, $f_0$ from
  the first readings, $k$ from the time at which most of the decline is over).
- Compare a random effect on $f_c$ with one on the whole curve, and explain the difference
  with the parallel curves on the log scale.
- Compare `steady`, `excess` and `both` and explain why the first two disagree.
- Report the ratio of depths with intervals and explain why the answer is "the data cannot
  tell" (and why that is a result).
